lessons.title: World Cup history
lessons.objective: You can name the eras of the World Cup.

payload.template: Brazil have won the World Cup {{times}} times, more than any other nation. Germany and Italy are next with {{next}} each.

explanation.correct: Right. Brazil have five titles (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002), with Germany and Italy on four each.
explanation.incorrect: Brazil hold the record with five World Cups. Germany and Italy have four each, so Brazil are the ones with five stars on the shirt.
explanation.sayThisLine: Brazil have five stars, the most World Cups of anyone.

payload.prompt: Match the World Cup moment to what happened.

pairs.definition: Uruguay hosted and won the very first World Cup.
Brazil won a third title, with Pelé leading the way.
France won the trophy on home soil.
Argentina and Messi beat France on penalties after a 3-3 final.

distractorDefinitions: England won the first World Cup and have never lost since.
Germany won the first ever World Cup in 1930.

explanation.summary: Four dates give you a quick tour: Uruguay at the start, Brazil in the Pelé years, France at home in 1998, and Argentina in Messi's big year.
explanation.sayThisLine: Uruguay started it, Brazil made it famous.

payload.prompt: Which country did Maradona lead to the World Cup in 1986?

options.text: Brazil
Argentina
Italy

explanation.correct: Right. Maradona won the World Cup with Argentina in 1986, one of the greatest individual performances in World Cup history.
explanation.incorrect: Maradona led Argentina to the World Cup in 1986. His influence was decisive throughout the tournament.
explanation.sayThisLine: Maradona took Argentina to the World Cup in 1986.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Pelé won three World Cups, nobody's ever done that again.

payload.question: What is this fan saying?

options.text: Pelé won three World Cup trophies
No other player has won three World Cups
Pelé is better than Messi and Ronaldo
Three World Cups is the GOAT standard

payload.translation: Pelé won the World Cup three times (1958, 1962, 1970), and no other player has done it. It is why his name comes up in every GOAT argument.

followUps.why: Lets her name recent history—Argentina and Messi.

followUps.line: Which World Cup do you remember best?
followUps.why: Gets her talking about a tournament she watched.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Use this to join a debate about the GOAT without claiming to know everything.

lessons.title: The 2026 World Cup
lessons.objective: You can talk about the 48-team World Cup and its final.

payload.prompt: Who won the 2026 World Cup final?

options.text: Argentina beat France on penalties
Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time
France beat Spain 2-1 in normal time

explanation.correct: Right. Spain won 1-0 after extra time; Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute. It was the first 48-team World Cup.
explanation.incorrect: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time at the 2026 World Cup. Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute.
explanation.sayThisLine: Torres in the 106th minute. Spain just won the whole thing.

payload.template: The 2026 tournament had {{teams}} teams in {{groups}} groups. The top {{top}} in each group plus the eight best third-placed teams reached the round of 32.

explanation.correct: Perfect. Twelve groups of four: the top two from each plus the eight best third-placed teams made a round of 32.
explanation.incorrect: Twelve groups of four, with the top two plus the eight best third-placed teams reaching the round of 32. That is 24 + 8 = 32 teams.

payload.prompt: What was new about the 2026 World Cup format?

options.text: It was held in the USA for the first time
It expanded from 32 to 48 teams
It introduced a league phase instead of straight knockout

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 World Cup was the first with 48 teams instead of 32. This gave more nations a shot at qualifying.
explanation.incorrect: For the first time, the World Cup had 48 teams (up from 32). The tournament was held across the USA, Canada and Mexico.
explanation.sayThisLine: Forty-eight teams at the World Cup, that's bigger than ever.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: More teams means more Cinderella stories, but also some really mismatched games.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Expansion brings underdog fairytale moments
It also risks lopsided matches
The 48-team format ruined the World Cup
Only big teams should qualify

payload.translation: The 48-team format gives smaller nations a real shot (fairness win) but means some teams are vastly outmatched (quality risk). Fans debate the trade-off.

followUps.line: Did the bigger field change how you watched the group stage?
followUps.why: Lets her share her own experience of the new format.
Gets her talking about exciting upsets.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can share the nuance—more teams is fairer but has downsides.

lessons.title: Ballon d'Or and GOAT
lessons.objective: You can discuss the individual-awards argument.

payload.prompt: The GOAT debate is mainly about...

options.text: Who scores the most goals in a year
How to weigh trophies, style, longevity and era
Who has the highest market value

explanation.correct: Right. The GOAT debate hinges on what you value: World Cups, Ballon d'Ors, era, longevity or style. Messi, Ronaldo, Pelé and Maradona each have a case.
explanation.incorrect: The GOAT debate weighs different greatness measures: trophies, individual awards, longevity, era and style. Goals alone do not settle it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The GOAT debate is basically about what you value most.

payload.template: The Ballon d'Or is given by {{who}}, and the winner is chosen by a vote of {{voters}}.

explanation.correct: Right. France Football magazine runs the Ballon d'Or, and journalists from around the world vote for it.
explanation.incorrect: The Ballon d'Or is France Football's award and journalists do the voting. FIFA has its own separate awards.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Ballon d'Or is France Football's award, the big individual prize.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The Ballon d'Or always causes a fight because everyone sees greatness differently.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Voters disagree on who deserves the award
Different people value different qualities in a player
The voting system is unfair
Only strikers should win the Ballon d'Or

payload.translation: The Ballon d'Or is voted on by journalists who each weigh "best player" differently: goals, trophies, big games or the whole year. Debate is guaranteed.

followUps.line: Who do you think deserved last year's award?
followUps.why: Lets her voice an opinion without claiming expertise.

followUps.line: Has your team's best player ever won it?
followUps.why: Gets her talking about her heroes.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Just know it's the top individual prize; debate about who deserves it is endless.

payload.title: The GOAT argument
payload.setting: She is defending her favourite in the GOAT debate.

exchanges.theirMessage: Messi's got to be the GOAT, right?

replies.text: He's got a case. World Cup, longevity, style—what do you weigh most?
replies.theirResponse: All of it, I guess. That's why it's so hard to choose.
Fair, but Ronaldo's got something to say too.

replies.text: Pelé won three World Cups, so it has to be him.
replies.theirResponse: Pelé had a case too, but you could say that about a few players.
replies.coachNote: Shutting her down instead of joining in; the debate is more fun as a shared one.

payload.closingNote: The GOAT debate has no single answer; enjoy weighing different views.

lessons.title: Famous derbies
lessons.objective: You can explain the great derbies.

payload.prompt: Match each famous derby to its rivalry.

pairs.definition: Real Madrid vs Barcelona, Spain's biggest fixture.
Manchester United vs Manchester City, the same city's two giants.
Arsenal vs Tottenham, neighbours who share a postcode and a grudge.
Rangers vs Celtic, the fierce Glasgow rivalry in Scotland.

distractorDefinitions: Bayern Munich vs Borussia Dortmund, often called Der Klassiker.
Juventus vs Inter, known as the Derby d'Italia.

explanation.summary: Each derby is defined by geography, history and identity, not just league position.
explanation.sayThisLine: These are the matches where city pride matters most.

payload.prompt: What makes a match a derby?

options.text: It's always between the top two teams in the league
It's a local rivalry with deep history and city pride
It's a cup final

explanation.correct: Right. A derby is a local rivalry (often same city) with deep history. Local pride matters as much as three points.
explanation.incorrect: A derby is a match between local rivals—teams from the same city or nearby. History and local pride define it.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's not just three points, it's the derby.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: In a derby, throw the form book out. Anything can happen.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Derby matches ignore normal form and prediction
Emotion and passion override quality in derbies
The worse team always wins a derby
Derbies are decided by referee mistakes

payload.translation: In derbies, history, passion and local pride create unpredictability. The underdog is more dangerous; surprises are common.

followUps.line: What's the biggest derby in her country?
followUps.why: Gets her talking about her own stakes.

followUps.line: Has the underdog ever won a big derby?
followUps.why: Lets her recall a surprise result.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Ask which derby matters most to her team; it's always personal.

payload.prompt: Match each city to its two clubs.

pairs.definition: Real Madrid and Atlético Madrid.
AC Milan and Inter.
Liverpool and Everton, the Merseyside derby.
Roma and Lazio, the Derby della Capitale.

distractorDefinitions: Turin: Juventus and Torino share the city.
Manchester: United and City share the city.

explanation.summary: Most big football cities are split between two clubs, which is where local derbies come from.
explanation.sayThisLine: Same city, different colours. That is a derby.

lessons.title: Bosman and the money era
lessons.objective: You can explain how the Bosman ruling changed transfers.

payload.prompt: The Bosman ruling (1995) changed transfers by allowing...

options.text: Clubs to demand higher fees from richer teams
Players to leave for free when their contract expired
Agents to negotiate for players without club permission

explanation.correct: Right. Bosman ruled that a player whose contract ended could move without a transfer fee. This gave players power and sent wages and fees soaring.
explanation.incorrect: The Bosman ruling let players move for free at contract expiry instead of being stuck. It gave players leverage and changed football's economics.
explanation.sayThisLine: Bosman changed everything, players finally had power.

payload.prompt: Complete the Premier League origin story.
payload.template: The Premier League began in {{year}}, when England's top clubs broke away from the {{body}} to sell their own TV rights.

explanation.correct: Right. The Premier League started in 1992 and turned English football into a global TV product.
explanation.incorrect: The Premier League began in 1992 when the top clubs left the Football League to run the top division themselves and sell the TV rights.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Premier League turned English football into a global TV show.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: After Bosman, player wages and transfer fees exploded because clubs had to compete for talent.

payload.question: What caused the explosion?

options.text: Players could walk away for free at contract end
Clubs had to pay higher salaries to retain stars
The Premier League became the richest league
Transfer fees were abolished after Bosman

payload.translation: Bosman gave players leverage: clubs had to pay higher wages to keep them or lose them for nothing. This created a transfer market arms race.

followUps.line: Did this help or hurt smaller clubs?
followUps.why: Lets her weigh fairness vs market forces.

followUps.line: How has this changed the game for your team?
followUps.why: Gets her thinking about her club's reality.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Say it shifted power to players and transformed football's economics.

pairs.definition: Freed players at contract end; gave them power and sent wages soaring.
England's top tier became a commercial global brand with TV deals.
British TV's investment in live football rights transformed club finances.
Asian and American investment brought new money into European clubs.

distractorDefinitions: FFP rules were introduced to limit spending and prevent debt.
Salary caps were introduced in all leagues to ensure parity.

explanation.summary: Bosman, the Premier League's commercialization and global TV investment created modern football's money dynamics.
explanation.sayThisLine: These changes turned football into a multi-billion-pound business.

lessons.title: Women's football
lessons.objective: You can tell the story of women's football and why the boom is recent.

payload.prompt: England's FA banned women's football from 1921 to...

explanation.correct: Right. The FA banned women's football from its member clubs' grounds from 1921 to 1971. The 1999 World Cup and the NWSL's 2013 launch later helped rebuild momentum.
explanation.incorrect: The ban ran from 1921 to 1971, fifty years. Growth was slow afterwards, and the 1999 World Cup and the NWSL (2013) helped rebuild momentum.
explanation.sayThisLine: The ban lasted fifty years and look at the crowds now.

payload.prompt: The 1999 Women's World Cup final drew about 90,000 fans to which stadium?

options.text: The Rose Bowl in California
Wembley in London
Camp Nou in Barcelona

explanation.correct: Right. The 1999 final at the Rose Bowl, with about 90,000 fans, showed the world women's football could fill huge stadiums.
explanation.incorrect: It was the Rose Bowl in the USA. That crowd was a watershed moment for women's football, and investment followed.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ninety thousand at the Rose Bowl in 1999, that changed minds.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Women's football was invisible for decades, then suddenly it exploded.

payload.question: What caused the sudden growth?

options.text: Investment and media coverage finally arrived
The quality of play improved dramatically
Sponsorship deals multiplied after 1999
Men's football declined, so women's rose

payload.translation: The 1999 World Cup proved there was an audience. Investment, TV deals and player profiles followed, and the NWSL's launch in 2013 helped speed things up.

followUps.line: Who is a player she knows?
followUps.why: Starts conversation about the game, not politics.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can link women's growth to investment and visibility, not moral argument.

payload.title: Women's football is growing
payload.setting: She is excited about the growth of women's football.

exchanges.theirMessage: The crowds are massive now. So different from ten years ago.

replies.text: It's wild how fast it's changed. What's the biggest moment you remember?
replies.theirResponse: The 2022 Euros final at Wembley. Almost ninety thousand people.
replies.coachNote: Shows you see the shift and asks for her memory.

replies.text: Women's football is the future, no doubt.
replies.theirResponse: I just like the game, regardless.
replies.coachNote: Overstate; she is about the sport, not politics.

payload.closingNote: She cares about the sport and investment in it. Ask what she wants to see next.

lessons.title: US soccer and the great seasons
lessons.objective: You can explain how soccer grew in the US and name benchmark seasons.

payload.prompt: Which of these marks a milestone in US soccer growth?

options.text: Pelé and the NASL in the 1970s
The 1994 World Cup hosted in the USA
David Beckham joining MLS in 2007

explanation.correct: All three. Pelé drew crowds in the 1970s. The 1994 World Cup showed America cared. Beckham in 2007 proved MLS could attract global stars.
explanation.incorrect: All three are milestones: Pelé in the 1970s, the 1994 World Cup, and Beckham's 2007 arrival all advanced US soccer.
explanation.sayThisLine: MLS started in 1996 after the World Cup proved America wanted soccer.

payload.prompt: What is the 'Invincibles' season in soccer?

options.text: Manchester United won everything in 1999
Arsenal went unbeaten in the 2003–04 Premier League
Liverpool won five European Cups in a row

explanation.correct: Right. Arsenal went through the entire 2003–04 Premier League unbeaten. It remains a landmark of dominance.
explanation.incorrect: Arsenal's 2003–04 season where they did not lose a single league match is called 'The Invincibles'. It is a benchmark achievement.
explanation.sayThisLine: Unbeaten all season, that's the Invincibles.

statement.speaker: Historian
statement.text: Arsenal's Invincibles and Man United's 1999 treble are held up as the gold standard of greatness.

payload.question: What makes these seasons special?

options.text: They won everything or nearly everything
They are benchmarks of dominance and excellence
They prove a team is better than all others
They are the only great seasons in modern football

payload.translation: Arsenal went unbeaten in 2003–04 ("Invincibles"). Man United won the league, FA Cup and European Cup in 1999 ("treble"). Both are referenced as peak achievement.

followUps.why: Gets her talking about what matters to her.

followUps.line: Is winning style as important as winning?
followUps.why: Invites debate on dominant vs scrappy wins.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Use these as reference points for excellence without claiming one is objectively best.

payload.prompt: Match these soccer achievements to their teams and years.

pairs.definition: Went unbeaten through the 2003–04 Premier League season.
Won the league, FA Cup and European Cup in 1999.
Won the 2010 World Cup and back-to-back Euros (2008, 2012).
Won multiple Champions Leagues and La Ligas in the 2000s–2010s.

distractorDefinitions: Real Madrid's record haul of European Cups.
Italy's four World Cups, level with Germany.

explanation.summary: Great seasons are benchmarks fans reference to weigh dominance, style and legacy.
explanation.sayThisLine: These are the seasons fans bring up when comparing all-time greatness.
